Task: Develop a complete lesson plan for teaching probability to high-school students.

High-School Mathematics Lesson Plan  
Topic: Foundations of Probability (1 × 55-minute period)

1. Lesson Overview  
Students will explore basic probability through hands-on experiments, visual models, and real-world contexts. They will compute theoretical and experimental probabilities, compare the two, and interpret results.

2. Learning Objectives (SWBAT – Students Will Be Able To)  
• Define key terms: experiment, outcome, sample space, event, probability (theoretical vs. experimental).  
• Calculate simple probabilities of single-stage events.  
• Conduct an experiment (coin-and-spinner game), record frequencies, and determine experimental probability.  
• Compare and explain differences between theoretical and experimental probabilities.  
• Communicate reasoning using appropriate mathematical vocabulary.

3. Standards Alignment  
• CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.HSS.IC.A.1 – Understand statistics as a process for making inferences.  
• CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.HSS.IC.A.2 – Decide if a specified model is consistent with results of a given data-generating process.  
• CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.HSS.MD.A.1 – Define a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events.

4. Materials & Technology  
• Smartboard or projector  
• PowerPoint / Google Slides deck  
• Class set: two fair coins & one 4-color spinner per pair (printable spinner + paperclip)  
• Student handout (definitions, tables, exit ticket)  
• Whiteboards & markers (optional)  
• Graphing calculators or Desmos (optional)  
• Timer

5. Prior Knowledge / Warm-Up (5 min)  
Bell-ringer on board:  
a) “What’s the probability of rolling a number greater than 4 on a standard die?”  
b) “What’s an example of something in everyday life that seems random?”  
Students answer individually, then share. Instructor collects misconceptions.

6. Direct Instruction & Guided Discovery (10 min)  
• Mini-lecture with visuals: vocabulary & formula P(A)=#favorable/ #possible.  
• Demonstrate very simple sample space (flipping one coin).  
• Pose question: “Will actual results always match the fraction ½? Why or why not?”

7. Activity 1 – Coin-and-Spinner Experiment (20 min)  
Set-up: Each pair flips two coins and spins the 4-color spinner 30 times. They record results in table:  
Outcome example: (Heads, Tails, Blue).  
Part A – Theoretical: Students list sample space size (2×2×4=16) and compute P(getting at least one Head and Blue).  
Part B – Experimental: Conduct 30 trials, tally frequencies, compute experimental probability for same event.  
Part C – Analysis: Partners calculate percentage error and discuss reasons for discrepancy (sample size, randomness).

8. Activity 2 – Whole-Class Simulation & Visualization (10 min)  
• Collect each pair’s experimental data quickly via Google Form or show of hands.  
• Project aggregated frequencies; compare class experimental probability to theoretical.  
• Discuss Law of Large Numbers informally.

9. Closure / Exit Ticket (5 min)  
Prompt: “In your own words describe the difference between theoretical and experimental probability and give an example when they might differ.”  
Students submit on half-sheet before leaving.

10. Assessment  
Formative: Warm-up responses, teacher circulation during activities, questioning.  
Summative: Exit ticket (graded) & homework problems.

11. Differentiation / Supports  
• ELL: Provide vocabulary sheet with visuals/icons.  
• SPED: Pre-highlighted handout with key formulas; offer to conduct only 15 trials.  
• Advanced: Challenge extension – Calculate probability of getting exactly two Heads and Green, then design an experiment to test it; optional homework on compound events and tree diagrams.

12. Homework (optional)  
Worksheet: 10 problems mixing dice, cards, marbles; 2 reflective questions on experimental vs theoretical probability. Online interactive Desmos activity link.

13. Anticipated Misconceptions & Remedies  
• Belief that probability guarantees outcomes – Emphasize randomness and sample size.  
• Adding vs multiplying probabilities – Provide tree diagram examples.  
• Experimental results “wrong” – Stress concept of approximation.

14. Extensions / Enrichment  
• Introduce mutually exclusive vs independent events next lesson.  
• Have students design their own carnival game and calculate house edge.

15. Reflection (Teacher Notes, post-lesson)  
Record: student engagement levels, timing adjustments, common misconceptions to revisit, and names of students needing re-teaching.

This lesson moves from concrete experimentation to abstract reasoning, builds vocabulary, and lays groundwork for deeper topics like compound probability and distributions.
